name: enum4linux
one_line: enumerate information from Windows and Samba systems
plain: `enum4linux` asks a Windows or Samba machine what it is willing to tell an anonymous visitor: user names, groups, shares, the password policy, the operating system and domain details. It wraps several Samba tools (smbclient, rpcclient, net, nmblookup) into one report.
It is the standard first look at SMB (ports 139/445) in a lab. A usernames list from it is the starting point for password attacks, and the password policy tells you how careful to be.
when: Collect user and group names from an SMB host.
List shares and the password policy.
Brute-force user names with RID cycling when direct listing is blocked.

examples.title: Everything simple
examples.explain: -a runs all the simple enumerations. The report is long; look for 'Users on', 'Share Enumeration' and 'Password Policy'.

examples.title: Shares
examples.explain: -S lists shares and tests which can be accessed.

examples.title: Password policy
examples.explain: -P shows lockout threshold and minimum length: key for deciding how many guesses are safe.

examples.title: With credentials
examples.explain: -u and -p provide a user; many more details appear when you are authenticated.

examples.title: RID cycling for users
examples.explain: -r finds users by walking relative identifiers when the direct list is blocked.

examples.title: Save the output
examples.explain: The report is long, so keep a copy.

examples.title: Modern replacement
examples.explain: enum4linux-ng is a maintained Python rewrite with JSON output and clearer results.

options.plain: Keep searching RIDs until N consecutive misses.
Brute-force share names from a file.
Known user, used with -r when connecting as a different user.
Verbose: show the commands being run.

mistakes: Reading only the first lines: the useful part is deep in the report.
Forgetting that anonymous access is often blocked on new Windows versions.
Trusting the output on its own: confirm with smbclient or rpcclient.
Using the unmaintained original for modern targets: try enum4linux-ng.
Running it on networks you do not own.
try: Run enum4linux -a on a lab Samba server and list the users.
Read the password policy and note the lockout threshold.
Compare with the output of nmap's smb-enum-* scripts.
see_also: smbclient(1), rpcclient(1), nmap(1), crackmapexec, nbtscan(1), ldapsearch(1), enum4linux-ng.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
